issues.legal_issue: An erroneous determination of a court’s statutory jurisdiction on a pure question of law does not bar reconsideration of that jurisdictional issue in a later proceeding between the same parties.
material_facts: A tenant leased open land to construct residential or business buildings, built on it, and applied to have the standard rent determined under the applicable rent-control law.
In an earlier proceeding between the same parties concerning the same land, the court held that the rent-control law did not apply and rejected the application for lack of jurisdiction.

The tenant later made a fresh application after a subsequent authoritative decision established that the law’s application depended on the terms of the lease and that such a building lease was not excluded solely because the land was open when let.
The courts below treated the earlier jurisdictional determination as res judicata.
The Supreme Court held that the earlier determination was erroneous and that treating it as conclusive would give it the effect of a special rule governing the court’s jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The earlier decision did not operate as res judicata. The appeals were allowed, the orders below were set aside, and the proceedings were remanded for determination according to law.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a decision by a competent court on an issue of fact or a mixed question of law and fact is generally final between the parties. A decision on a question of law may also bind the parties when the cause of action is the same, but not where the question concerns the court’s jurisdiction, the cause of action differs, the law has since changed, or the decision sanctions an illegal transaction. Res judicata is a rule of procedure and cannot displace the law governing jurisdiction. The Court relied on Tarini Charan Bhattacharjee v. Kedar Nath Haldar and Broken Hill Proprietary Company Ltd. v. Municipal Council of Broken Hill, approved Parthasardhi Ayyangar v. Chinnakrishna Ayyangar, Chamanlal v. Bapubhai, and Kanta Devi v. Kalawati, disapproved Chandi Prasad v. Maharaja Mahendra Mahendra Singh, and doubted the relevant part of Bindeshwari Charan Singh v. Bageshwari Charan Singh. It also relied on Mrs. Dossibai N. B. Jeejeebhoy v. Khemchand Gorumal in finding the earlier jurisdictional decision erroneous.

predicates.later_proceeding_between_same_parties: The parties to an earlier proceeding bring a later proceeding against each other concerning the issue previously decided.
predicates.prior_decision_on_pure_jurisdictional_la: The earlier court decided, as a pure question of law, whether it had authority to hear the matter.
predicates.prior_jurisdiction_ruling_was_erroneous: The earlier court’s determination of its authority was contrary to the law governing that authority.
predicates.jurisdictional_issue_not_barred_by_res_j: The earlier determination does not prevent the jurisdictional issue from being considered in the later proceeding.

issues.definition: When parties bring a later proceeding after an erroneous decision on a pure question of the earlier court’s authority, that decision does not prevent the jurisdictional issue from being considered again.
